title: The king with ten heads
hookLine: Ravana weighs wise advice against his sister's rage; ahamkara, the ego
carry: ahamkara: the ego shouts over wisdom
last: GOD COMES DOWN WHEN DHARMA FALLS.

cards: Lanka, the golden city. On the throne sits Ravana. Ten heads.
Twenty arms. Before you picture a cartoon monster, hear what the tradition says about him. He's brilliant: a great scholar of the Vedas, a master musician, a devoted worshipper of Shiva.
Once, the story goes, he tried to lift Shiva's mountain, got his arm pinned under it, and roared so loud that Shiva named him Ravana, the one who roars, or makes the world cry.
A king of enormous power and enormous learning. And the messenger from the forest kneels in front of him: Khara is dead. His army is gone.

teach.h: TAKE HIS WIFE, THE MESSENGER SAYS.
teach.b: The messenger adds a suggestion: you can't beat Rama in battle, but he has a wife, Sita, the most beautiful woman in the world. Take her, and he'll die of grief. Ravana likes the idea.
He rides to an old rakshasa living as a hermit: Maricha.
Maricha tells Ravana plainly: don't. Rama is not someone you want as an enemy. And, remarkably, Ravana listens.
He goes home. It could have ended there. Then Shurpanakha walks into his court, disfigured and blazing.
In Valmiki she doesn't just ask for revenge; she humiliates him in front of everyone.
What kind of king are you, lying around in luxury while men cut up your sister and kill your army? Then she describes Sita. That does it.
Notice what kind of mistake this is. Ravana isn't stupid. He heard the good advice and even followed it for a day.
Hindu teaching has a name for what beat it: ahamkara, the ego.

teach.h: AHAMKARA: THE EGO SHOUTS OVER WISDOM.
teach.b: Literally, the I-maker: the part of you that makes everything about me, my honor, my insult. Some teachers read Ravana's ten heads as ten faults, anger, greed, pride and the rest, all talking at once.
His learning didn't save him. The ego heard 'you've been insulted' louder than 'this is a terrible mistake'.
That's why, at Dussehra, when huge effigies of Ravana go up in flames, many Hindus say they're burning something in themselves too.

how: At Dussehra many Hindus burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana; many also remember him as a learned devotee of Shiva, and some communities honor him in their own ways.

o: Ravana sends Rama a message of peace
Ravana prays to Shiva and hears his blessing
Ravana gets the news, and pride makes the choice

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: what kind of king are you?

s: the tradition paints Ravana as a stupid brute
he's a great scholar, a musician and a devotee of Shiva.
Ravana first follows Maricha's advice and goes home
until Shurpanakha shames him in his own court.
Ravana's name was given by Shiva
after he roared, pinned under Shiva's mountain, the story says.

games.q: you're Ravana. Maricha says leave Rama alone. your sister says you're weak. which voice is ahamkara, the ego?
o: the one that says: you've been insulted, prove you're strong.
the one that says: leave Rama alone.
games.why: ahamkara, the I-maker, makes it all about my honor. Ravana chose that voice, and it cost him everything.

practice: Think of a time you knew the right thing and did the other thing because someone made you feel small. Give that voice its name: ahamkara, the I-maker. If you pray, offer it to God, the way Hindus give Ravana to the Dussehra fire.
If not, just watch it for two minutes, and notice that the wise voice is quieter, and still there.

wordCard.voice: Ravana hears. The ten-headed king of Lanka ignores Maricha's warning and heeds his sister's rage, and decides to take Sita.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ten (dasha) faced (anana), a name of Ravana.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara, the ego shouts over wisdom. Ravana had heard the right voice first. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 31–35 (Akampana's report; Maricha's warning; Shurpanakha in Ravana's court)
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 16 (Ravana under Mount Kailash; his name)
